utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Kuo: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphones are off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you turn the witness's microphones on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, at the end of the day yesterday, I was asking you about your knowledge of things going on around town and you wanted to know what specifically I meant, so I'll ask you some specific questions today. You knew that the mosques in Foca were all being destroyed, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was obvious that they were destroyed; yes, one could see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also knew that Muslim men were being rounded up and taken first to Livade and then to the KP Dom, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those in KP Dom, them I saw. And as for those in Livade, I heard from them, that is from some of them, that they had been to Livade. As I mentioned, Mr. Suvalija and another lady doctor, Asima, it's from her that I heard that, from her it was that I heard they had been to Livade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you also knew that the doctors had been arrested from the Foca hospital and taken into detention, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of them, yes, I saw in the KP Dom, and I know that that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also know that Muslim flats were being searched at this time, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I learned that afterwards. I didn't know it at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You learned also that Muslims were being beaten on occasion when they were arrested, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that, because I could not know it or see it. Only one heard rumours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You learned about it from other people, that people -- that Muslims were being beaten in Foca at this time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also learned that Muslim women and girls were detained in the Partizan Sports Hall and the Foca high school during this time, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard that they were brought there in order to be taken to other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You learned also that soldiers, Serb soldiers, came to those places and took the women and girls out and raped them, right? You learned about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never heard anything being said in Foca at that time about what was happening in the Partizan Sports Hall?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, because I really -- and I must tell you one thing here, I had my regular routine route; home, work, work, home, and I hardly ever went out to see some people, to socialise with anyone, I mean anyone that I could hear anything like that from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your son Dubravko was working in the reserve police force at this time, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The police station is right next to the Partizan Sports Hall; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never heard from your son Dubravko about what was happening at the Partizan Sports Hall with the women and girls there? About the soldiers that would come and take them out?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, because I had very little contact with my Dubravko since my house had burned down and he had his own family, his wife and children, and he lived with his father-in-law in Gornje Polje. So that we'd meet only in passing and say hello one to another, or now and then, if he had time, he'd come to our flat, but believe me, we never talked about that. So that I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that Muslims were fleeing Foca at this time out of fear, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say if they were fleeing for fear but I know they were leaving in buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by the middle of August, 1992, most of the Muslims had left through one means or another, either by fleeing individually or in buses organised by the government, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that was the middle or the end of August, whatever, but yes, we learned that most of them had left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, the Sabanovics, the mother and daughter whom you helped, were quite desperate to get out of Foca and scared to stay there, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea who that family is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The family whom the -- Desanka Bogdanovic referred to you. You don't know their names?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I do not know what their last name is, but they left sometime in early June because it happened right after the misfortune that struck me and that was the early June, that is end of May, early June, sometime about then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to make sure we are talking about the same incident. Desanka Bogdanovic approached you about a mother and daughter, Muslims, who were quite desperate to leave Foca, and she asked for your help and you arranged for a car and a driver to leave in the early morning hours so that they could escape Foca. This is the incident that we are talking about, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I want to make sure that we got this right; this was -- the translation shows that you said this happened right after the misfortune that befell you, and I assume that you're talking about when your son lost his legs. It happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry, that's why I'm saying it happened before, before the misfortune struck my sons, and it was then that I did a favour to -- because Mrs. Desanka had asked me to and she then did the favour for those two friends, that is, she put those two women in my son's car and it took them to Scepan Polje, but she told me that she were going to meet with their family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made the arrangements for the driver to pick up these two women early in the morning, around 6.30 or 7.00, and you did that because it was safer to do that, right, rather than the middle of the day?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can draw your own conclusions as you please, but I simply thought it more convenient because I had to be at my workplace at 7.00 so that to do -- so that I had to turn over my son's car to the driver and yet make it to work at 7.00. Besides, I think that there was a curfew on and one could not go out before 6.00, so it could have been sometime after 6.00, half or 20 past 6.00, perhaps around half past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that when the women got into the car, they hid under their luggage so they couldn't be seen, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They squatted and didn't sit down. I didn't give it a thought at that time, nor do I think about it this time. Perhaps they thought they ought to hide while passing through the town because, as you leave Gornje Polje, you have to go through the town in order to go on to Scepan Polje, so that their travel bags, rather than to put them behind, they put them on the seats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It must have been obvious to you that they were trying to hide and not be seen as they tried to leave Foca, right? It's not the normal way people sit in a car.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Desanka asked me and told me that I was the only one she could tell about it, then, yes, there must be some truth in this, that they also had to be hidden from view somehow, not to be seen. And I didn't ask them if they had any documents, any certificates authorising them to leave; believe me, I never paid any attention to that. It was up to me to provide the car and transport, that is, the driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The way in which the two women left in the car, plus the reaction of Desanka Bogdanovic, that she was so scared and could only trust you, those things led you to conclude that the two Muslim women were scared and wanted to leave Foca and could only leave Foca secretly, right? That was the only conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a kind of conclusion that I can draw now, that it was something like that, because she also did it surreptitiously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that Foca was not a safe place for Muslims at this time, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that nobody was safe in Foca at that time, Serbs or Muslims. I do not know if I said that before, but in Foca and around Foca -- well, not in the town itself but around Foca fighting went on until one could say 1994, because take, for instance, the end of 1992, what happened 9 kilometres away from Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me -- the question was only about Foca itself. You understood that it was unsafe for Muslims in Foca specifically because you even offered to transport the third woman, another Muslim woman, her name was Nedziba Sirbubalo, who was present during this time. You even offered to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have her transported out, if necessary, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can't remember. What third woman?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were present during the testimony of Mrs. Bogdanovic, right? And you heard her testify --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I have to interrupt. But so as not to misinterpret, Mr. Krnojelac's answer, when my learned friend asked about the third person, the interpreter did not know the name, could not hear the name, and Mr. Krnojelac did not have the name of that third person, so I suppose you did not know it but I simply want -- or hope that you will not misinterpret his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean the name was not interpreted into B/C/S? It's certainly not in the transcript either, I'm afraid. You made a very valiant effort at the pronunciation, but you'd better have another go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I'm trying to approach it in a more descriptive way because it may be that Mr. Krnojelac doesn't actually know her name either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You may as well give it a go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nedziba Sirbubalo. There was a third woman who was present when the mother and daughter were taken out of Foca and there was testimony by one of your witnesses that, when everybody was saying goodbye, there was another Muslim woman there who did not leave that day but that you offered -- you told Mrs. Bogdanovic that you would help transport that third Muslim woman out, if necessary. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there were Mrs. Bogdanovic and other two Muslim women and Desa Bogdanovic was the third one. I do not remember any other woman or having promised anything. That there was somebody, and that I had promised something to somebody, I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you never told Mrs. Bogdanovic that you would help another Muslim woman escape, even though eventually it wasn't necessary?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had Desa asked me again to do it, I would have done it again, but at that time, I do not remember promising anything to anyone, but anything's possible in life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you knew at this time that there were other prison camps being set up in other municipalities where Muslim men were detained, right? KP Dom was not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 18th of April when I arrived there, all I knew about was the KP Dom, and that part of people who were brought from Livade and others who were arrested around the town. I didn't know about any others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your time as the warden of KP Dom, you went to meetings with the Ministry of Justice, and you learned that there were other prison camps set out in other municipalities where Muslim men were detained, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other municipalities? I knew it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 27th or 28th of April 1992, you were present in the KP Dom, around 3.00 in the morning when a JNA officer, a Muslim, was brought in from the Filipovici fuel depot, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know - and I wasn't in the KP Dom at the time, I'm sure of that - and that officer wasn't brought to the KP Dom. He was brought, and I learned it later, what, that one officer had been brought with a group of soldiers and put above the canteen near the -- in the vicinity of the KP Dom, not inside the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The officer that I'm referring to was a Muslim officer, and you knew both his brothers. Are we talking about the same person?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew his late father and I knew one of his brothers. I didn't know his other brother. And he was put up above the canteen, not within the compound of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You allowed this officer to make a phone call to his brother in Sarajevo, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember, believe me, that I let him, but if he did ask me, then I think I did it for him. All I know is that we had coffee together one morning because he asked me, "May I have a cup of coffee with you?" Yes, sure, why not? And we had this coffee in the room, in that office of mine that I'm telling you was called censorship earlier, and I didn't think that he had been taken in or that he was in prison, because he was accommodated with some soldiers in that part of the restaurant where there were rooms for visits of families to the convicts before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you had coffee that morning with that officer, he had just been brought in and there was a soldier named Dida, a Serb soldier who was shooting wildly and threatening to kill a busload of refugees if he wasn't paid. Surely you'd remember that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you I was not there. I was not present at all, and I heard that it happened in the evening hours and that they spent one night, that is, that the military had put a group of women and children in the KP Dom, women and children brought over from Filipovici. I put them in that part where all the other Muslims were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They didn't ask you permission to do that, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened at night and nobody asked any permission because the KP Dom had already been let -- that is, I do not know if there was any -- whether it had indeed been rented out to the army but the military were already there and I was not present then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came in the morning and had coffee with that officer in the censorship room, you learned that the women and children had been kept overnight inside the KP Dom, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I didn't have that coffee with him the very next morning. It was a bit later on because this officer and those troops were there for several days. It wasn't that morning that I had coffee with him, but afterwards, I learnt from a guard, I can't remember which one, that that group of women and children had spent the night there and that the next day they had been taken away from the KP Dom. So they only spent one night there and then they were taken away from the KP Dom; where and how, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who put them in the KP Dom compound?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there and I do not know who put them there. I was told that it was the army who had brought them there, that is, those White Eagles, or was it the guards? Well, be that as it may, it was the military who brought them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but in the transcript, if my English is good enough, it should be guards means -- means watchmen and the witness said White Eagles or the guard. 24th line, page ten, line 24, guard with capital G.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But are you worried about the number? It's reported as having said the guards, plural. You think there was only the singular? Is that the problem you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Again, perhaps my English is not good enough, but as it says here, the guards, what the witness indicated was the name of the formation, the Guard, that is what it was called, and the witness said the White Eagles or the Guard. Guard is a separate military formation. We've heard about the White Eagles, we've heard all about the Serb Guards as another military formation. The witness did not say guardsmen, watchmen; he meant the Guard or perhaps the Serb Guard as another military formation; the name of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will get it sorted out. I think, Ms. Kuo, I've thought of "the guard" or "the guards" as meaning the non-military people working inside the jail, so that we'd better get what the witness intended sorted out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I asked you who put these women and children in the KP Dom, and you answered that it was the army who brought them there, that is, those White Eagles or was it the guard, could you tell us what you meant by "the guard"? Did you mean a military or non-military unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I learned that they had been brought there. I'm not sure, I don't remember what did they say, that it was the White Eagles or the so-called Serb Guard, and I wasn't there so I cannot really know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The time that the women and children were brought into the KP Dom was when the JNA officer was also brought in, right? The same time, because they had all come from Filipovici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they came together or not, but I think that it was that same day or, rather, that same night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the end of April, the 27th or 28th, before the contract that part of the KP Dom would be let out to the military, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember the exact date, but in that case, it was the Uzice unit that was on guard duty then. If I had been there, believe me, I would not have stood up to them. They came there before I did, and I could not have stood up to them in the sense of why were they doing something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in charge of the entire KP Dom at that time, right? There had been no contract that any part of it was going to be let out to the military, was there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, they were running the part where they were staying, or rather, the entire KP Dom, precisely the guards from Uzice. I was only with the commission going round taking the inventory and registering all the damage that had been sustained, so I had no right to enter their premises. They wouldn't let me. And that is why there were those negotiations with Mr. Mladjenovic that it could not be done that way, that I was to guard the property, to safeguard the property, and then others are there since that part was rented out, and he said to me, "Milorad, somebody has to safeguard this property from these people who are there."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, on the 25th of May 1992, a bus arrived from Bar in Montenegro, carrying Muslims and Serbs to the -- carrying Muslims and Serbs, and about 25 Muslims were brought into the KP Dom, many of whom were beaten on their way in. You were present at that time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that I was not present, but I did hear that people from Montenegro were brought in. I don't know when they were brought in, at what time of the day or I don't even know the date or something like that. It was in May, though, because there is no reason for me not to tell you that I had been present and seen that. I would have told you had I been present and had I seen it, but I wasn't. I don't even know what time of day they arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did learn of this group being brought in, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out a few days later from one of these guards, because at that time, there were quite a few guards there who had already arrived, those who had worked in the KP Dom before, and I was really surprised by this bus. They were talking about it, the guards, and they said that there were also Serbs who were brought from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember which of the guards that was? You said you learned this from one of the guards. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't remember, but most probably it was one of those whom I knew better from before the conflict. I really can't remember who said this, because usually this would just be mentioned in passing, very fast. It wasn't like you're sitting and chatting with someone for an hour or two. Somebody said, yeah, they came, they brought in Muslims and Serbs and there are even Croats there, and it's mentioned and that's it. Now, for me to remember, I ask you kindly to try to understand, after all these years, it's hard for me to remember people's names and various moments, but I did hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you knew that in the months of April, May and even June, Muslim men were being brought into the KP Dom in large numbers, right? Several hundred?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I learned, I learned from other people. I did not see anything with my very own eyes. It was known that people were brought in but I did not see anything with my very own eyes. I would have to remember had I seen it, but really, I had so many other obligations, because what could I see if on that day I went to the farm at Brioni or Maglic or the warehouses, Perucica, places like that. I would enter through the gate to the right to the administration building --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you learned the number of Muslim detainees by talking to the cook and the warehouse keeper, right? You told the investigators that you did know the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The warehouse keeper once, or perhaps not only once, several times, said to me, "There are more people at the KP Dom and we need more food and we have to provide that food." But I always said that it was up to the military to provide that and they went there to ask them for it, and what was obtained was obtained. Because the military was supposed to provide food for detained persons, just like they got a cook, because I had nothing to do with this, and as I said, what I gave, I gave because some kind of stocks were obtained somehow, and people from the administration were eating at the same mess where they were eating, that one meal, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the military cook. That one cook provided food for everybody in the KP Dom, civilian and military alike, right? You didn't have your own separate civilian cook, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. One cook, and everything was cooked in one cauldron, as far as I know, because there wasn't any electricity, and that cauldron was outside and, in passing, as I would go to breakfast or to the furniture factory, I would see this cooking taking place in one and the same cauldron. How it was distributed, I don't know. I didn't attend their lunches and dinners. We from the administration, the clerks, we would usually take meals after them. They would have breakfast and then they would go to their accommodation and then we would come to a different dining room for breakfast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they," they would have their breakfast and then go to their accommodation before you ate, who did you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to detained persons of all three ethnicities, and also those people who were serving their sentences, three, four, five, it depended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you were in charge of providing food for everybody at the KP Dom, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Please, I was not in charge. The only thing I was in charge of was doing my own job, not to repeat what that was, but I was not in charge of providing food for them. However, as much as I could, I tried, as much as possible, when there were barters and also with the Red Cross and even some companies, I tried to obtain as much as I could because, after the good life that existed before the war, it is only natural that there was very little food, and it was difficult to get food, and I tried to get as much food as possible but I was not in charge of that. I'm asserting that to you because I would not have been looking for that -- am I talking too much? No, I was not in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Most of the time, a yes or no answer is sufficient. There wasn't a separate warehouse for the military detainees, was there? There was one warehouse that was shared by everybody. That provided food, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a separate warehouse in front of the kitchen, and as far as I know, food was stored there that was obtained from the military or, rather, from their rear in Livade. The other warehouse for food and equipment was below that building, was it number 1? At any rate, when you enter the gate, the compound, it's the warehouse over there, and I don't know that the food was not kept separately, that there was one and the same warehouse. No, I don't know about that, the food being kept in one and the same warehouse, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you kept track of how much food was needed for the detainees in the KP Dom as well as the convicts; is that right? You might not like the word "in charge of" but you certainly knew and were involved in that food supply, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not keep any records as to how much food was needed. The head of the kitchen kept records as to what he needed and in which quantities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went to the military, or you sent letters to the military, asking them for specific amounts of food for the detainees; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the kitchen would tell the warehouse keeper how much he needed, the warehouse keeper would send that to me, I would send it to the rear at Livade, and they were in charge of providing food. So I would send those papers to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were involved in securing food for the detainees, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually said that during barters, I obtained food, but for humanitarian purposes because of my humanitarian attitude towards them. By no means was this based on an obligation that I had to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in direct contact with the military with regard to food for the detainees, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in direct contact with the military in that respect. It was only paperwork, and that is not a direct contact. Resolving things through paperwork is not direct contact for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like to have the witness shown Exhibit D105.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, this is a letter written and signed by you, dated February 1993, to the Foca Tactical Group, as well as to the municipal assembly of Foca, the executive committee of the Foca municipal assembly, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't see this well but I believe what you're saying, and also I think it has to involve the rear, the command for the rear, and that this should have been addressed to them as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there is one line that is shown as illegible in the English translation so it's possible that that's where the rear that you're talking about should be addressed. But I'd like to ask you about the contents of this letter. About halfway through the first paragraph, there is the sentence that says, "The assistance provided by the military organs consisted of occasional help in foodstuffs which was insufficient to cover the aforementioned costs." And you go on to ask that there be regular allocations, that there be regular allocation of foodstuffs for "our needs." And in the very same letter, you talk about -- you ask for an allocation of a monthly ration of 100 litres of petrol for the needs of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I did not say that there wasn't paperwork involved, and that we did not have that kind of contact and that I did not ask for things that way. But I certainly found out about that from the head of the kitchen who said, through the warehouse keeper, that food was not arriving regularly, and I wanted to remind them of their duty, that they were duty-bound to provide these supplies regularly. As for petrol, I referred to that because that had to be transported as well because foodstuffs could not be carried on one's back. There weren't any horses so it could not be brought on horses either. That is why vehicles had to be used for transporting food and that is why we needed petrol. So I felt it was necessary for me to say what one person said to the other, that is, to say what the head of the kitchen said to the warehouse keeper and what the warehouse keeper said to me, and I felt it was necessary that I should write about that, and I do say at the very end, as a matter of fact, "We are counting on your understanding and help." If that's a bad thing to do, I mean --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to have the witness shown Exhibit D107. This is another letter signed by you, this one dated 3rd March 1993, addressed to the Foca Garrison military post, 7141. And here, you ask for -- you discuss how the KP Dom holds Muslim detainees and Serbian offenders from the army, and you ask for approval of the allocation of a list of food supplies, a very specific list, including beans and rice and macaroni in very specific amounts, and then you state, "These quantities are sufficient for a month's food requirements," right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, but this was compiled by the head of the kitchen according to the tables he had, according to the number of people involved, which he probably had, and then he compiled this kind of list. So then I asked for this and I forwarded it to the military authorities, because it is said here that there are detained persons of Muslim and Serb ethnicity, so if that's a crime, it is for the Honourable Court to judge, but it is true that, yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krnojelac, when you learned from the warehouse keeper that there was a shortage of food with regard to the detainees, you never went to any of the people that you have described as actually being in charge at the KP Dom; the military, the so-called military representatives. You didn't go to them, did you? You wrote letters directly to the command.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My best cooperation was in the fact that I wrote. For me to go without writing, it would have been pointless, and had I not written this, there would not have been these documents nowadays, but then, excuse me, you would not have believed what I have been telling you had these documents not been found. I did not go any farther than the rear that was in Livade, that is about two or two and a half kilometres away from KP Dom. It's not only that I asked them for this. I also asked for food at other companies and also in the Red Cross, and sometimes it actually turned out that I would get some food from the Red Cross too. Because there was the lady who was the boss there, Sneja [phoen], she was a pupil of mine before, and whenever there was food that was not distributed to refugees and displaced persons, she gave it to me. It was always welcome, whatever you could get; 20 litres of oil, 20 litres of oil, that's fine. Also, sometimes I could even get lard but I always kept looking for oil because Muslims did not want to eat food that was cooked on lard. So then I always had to look for oil.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, Mitar Rasevic was not involved in providing food for the detainees, was he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mitar Rasevic had a different duty in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Savo Todovic was not involved in providing food for the detainees, was he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he also had his other affairs. I don't know whether he was in contact with the command with regard to this food, but he also knew what the situation at the KP Dom was like in respect of food, because he probably went to these meals too, breakfast, that is, and he probably found out from the cook, but I really don't know whether he asked for anything and whether he contacted people for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you knew how many Muslim detainees were being kept at the KP Dom because you had access to the roll call notebooks and lists that were kept in the prisoners' quarters, right? There was one desk at the entrance to each prisoner quarter, and in the drawer of the desk was a list of the detainees and the daily roll calls, listing who was there and how many people, so you knew how many people were there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I did not know, and I wish you could tell me on the basis of what I could have known, because such documents were not accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you had access to labour provided by the Muslim detainees, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask it this way: Labour was scarce in the KP Dom and in all of Foca at this time, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And according to your testimony, you were expected to keep the functions of the Drina Economic Unit going during this time, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in order to keep this economic unit going, you needed workers, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly they were needed, yes, you could say that they were needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before the war, the labour supply for the Drina Economic Unit was provided by the prison population, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for civilian persons, there were civilian persons who worked in the Drina Economic Unit before the war and there were also convicted persons who were working there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You asked Mr. Mladjenovic for help securing craftsmen from the civilian population outside the prison population, right? And you got some people.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few carpenters were provided for the furniture factory but that was done by way of assignment to work obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But those people were not enough to keep the Drina Economic Unit going, right? You needed more workers than that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, what I needed the most was two extra men, head of the varnishing shop and a worker to do upholstery. However, they didn't send them. And then they sent people for cleaning the furniture factory - I think I already mentioned this - five or six people, detainees of Muslim ethnicity, who worked in that factory, together with these carpenters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is what I'm getting to, Mr. Krnojelac. The -- in order to keep the economic unit running, you requested to have some of the detainees available to work, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not the way it was. I did not ask for detained persons to be given to me. I asked for a head of the varnishing shop and also a craftsman who could do upholstery. Since they did not provide me with them, they gave these five or six people probably, who knew something about carpentry or perhaps they were carpenters, I don't know. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, let me take you through this step by step. In order to get the economic unit going, you needed people to help you and you made specific requests for people to help you, right? You don't need to go through it again but that's what you did; you made the requests for what -- who was needed.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, civilians, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were told that you could not get civilians, there were not enough people, civilians, in Foca to meet your needs, and that's why you were given detainees, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is why Mr. Todovic gave a list and said that those people were available and then, at a meeting of the board, I told so the heads of work units, namely that Mr. Todovic had that list and that they should turn to him and he'd give them those men from the detention unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you mentioned a meeting of the board. Can you tell us what board you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean -- well, I call it the board of directors; that is, head of the factory, head of the metal working, head of the farm, head of the commercial department, accountant, those people, people who were in charge of individual units, economic units, of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a meeting that Mr. Todovic also attended, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Todovic did not attend the meeting. He had informed me a day or two before that that he had received an order to that effect and I told Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. him that I'd tell people about it, or rather, that I'd tell heads of work units about it, and that they -- and that he should then talk to them and ask them how many men each of them needed. But I should like to add that on that occasion, I asked Mr. Todovic, "Tell me, please, are these people who are volunteering to work?" And he answered, "Yes, they are volunteering, and there are many more volunteers but they lack skills."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you mentioned an order that Mr. Todovic received. Can you tell us what that order was or what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought it was something oral or perhaps in writing, I don't know, but perhaps he was orally told to draw up this list of crafts, of skills, that is, what kind of skills those people had, and what kind of work could they do. That is what I meant, to simply write out a list of jobs, of skills.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn from whom he received this order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the military command, I suppose, from the Tactical Group. And the individual who did it, no, I didn't see him, and I didn't ask him, but since it was -- it belonged to the military part of the Tactical Group which was at Velecevo, that is as likely as not, in that women's part of the prison that formerly belonged to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom did you make the request for craftsmen?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mladjenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Mladjenovic didn't give you a direct response, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mladjenovic said that he'd see about it and do whatever he could do, because he realised that I needed them. I wouldn't have asked for them had I not needed them, especially those particular craftsmen, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear on that, you made your request to Mr. Mladjenovic and the next thing you heard was Mr. Todovic telling you that he could make a list of detainees who were available to work for you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the conversation with Mladjenovic. This conversation with Todovic occurred after the conversation with Mladjenovic, that he had those men available. What I needed most was the head of the varnishing department, because there were about 100 bookshelves that needed varnishing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us about the varnishing company several times; we really don't need to hear about that again. You also supervised the metalwork shop, right? And Mr. Relja Goljanin was in charge?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was put in charge of the whole Drina business unit and that included the metal working shop, but Relja was specifically in charge. He was the head of that work unit of the metal working shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people who were working for Mr. Goljanin in the metalwork shop were skilled workers, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't -- I wouldn't say that they worked for Mr. Goljanin. They worked in the metal shop and they were skilled workers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point, in May or June of 1992, a group of Muslim detainees was taken out of the KP Dom, some of whom worked in the metalwork shop, and Mr. Goljanin found out and got very angry that his workers, or workers in the metalwork shop, were being taken away. Do you recall that? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that Mr. Hamdo left the metal shop, and as for the others, no, nobody notified me nor do I know who went away from the metalwork shop, either to be exchanged or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a time when a list of the skilled metal shop workers was kept at the front gate, indicating that they were skilled workers and never to be taken out for exchange or anything else, right? Because they were needed in the KP Dom. There was such a list, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw it, nor am I aware of its existence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you know that the skilled workers working in the metalwork shop worked there throughout their detention, right, specifically because they had the skills that were necessary. They didn't rotate in and rotate out; they were a fixed group of people who were there for several months, working, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The metal working shop's task was maintenance. The maintenance. And apart from that, they finished, I think, two kiosks which were about to be completed, and the only task of the metal shop was to maintain buildings, that is, facilities, of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, please answer the question. The question was: Wasn't it true that this was a fixed group of detainees working there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew Ekrem Zekovic worked in the metalwork shop for several months throughout his detention, right? He was a familiar person to you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't know Ekrem all that well but I went there very seldom, or perhaps I would enter the metal shop but he'd be in a different workshop and then I wouldn't see him at all because I didn't go to all the workshops, there was no need for me to go into every nook and corner of that metal shop. I come up and pass by, so I don't know if there was this group or if there was a precise group. No, it couldn't be. And I learned that from Relja. Whenever I went there, he'd tell me they have taken Hamdo away; so it wasn't a fixed group, it changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Relja would tell you that they had taken something or someone away but the translation wasn't very clear. Can you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said there wasn't always the same number of people because he'd tell me after they had taken -- well, sometimes he'd tell me, sometimes he wouldn't. If they took somebody away, he'd tell me, "They have taken Hamdo away and I don't know whether they will bring him back," and one knew that it was the troops from Miljevina who took them away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Hamdo that you're referring to was taken to Miljevina to work on cars there, as a mechanic, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he did up there, I never asked him, and I don't know what he did, but, yes, true, he was a car mechanic, and a good one, both man and craftsman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you also knew Muhamed Lisica who worked for a long time in the metalwork shop, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew one another - well, not for a long time, I wouldn't say that - but I knew him, I knew him by sight mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned, gave a description of several of the things that were being made at the metalwork shop. Things being made there had to be approved by you or Mr. Goljanin, right? You couldn't do any unauthorized work in the metalwork shop, could you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relja Goljanin could authorise anything he liked, because at a meeting of yet another board, or another meeting of the board of directors, we had said that it would be very nice indeed if both the furniture factory and the metal shop could do so-called loan deals. You know what it is; it's something like maintenance, you are paid to do something. Yes, Mr. Goljanin could indeed authorise something like that except that an invoice had to be written out for that, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was -- you described the board meeting where this was made known. This was a decision that you made as a manager that they should be able to have some flexibility in authorising specific jobs, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no written decision. It was just a verbal arrangement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what I mean is, since you were in charge of the Drina Economic Unit, that was your decision to give your managers some flexibility, right? It wasn't something they just came up with on their own; you approved it.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree but it also -- that is how it was before, and I didn't want to deny them anything that they had before. And on my part, it was that in order to create a better and nicer atmosphere in that team of people who cooperated, to contribute to better understanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the invoice that you refer to meant that if the metalwork shop was contracted to do work for somebody outside the KP Dom, that that person or company would be billed for the work, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw any invoice, because it wasn't brought to me. If there was any, it wouldn't be brought to me, it was turned over to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We really must focus on answering the question. My question wasn't whether you saw the invoice. You made reference to an invoice and I was simply asking you what that meant. When you said "the invoice," all it meant was a bill that would be sent to whoever from outside the KP Dom the work was being done for, right? That's all you meant.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know if there were any invoices. I do not know if they did any work for anyone outside the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you stated Mr. Goljanin could authorise something like that, "except that an invoice had to be written out for that, of course." So the agreement was that the metalwork shop could do outside work but that a bill had to be sent to whoever that work was being done for, right? That was the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this invoice is then given not to the manager of the economic unit but to the administration so that they could do the calculations and then send the bill for the work done. That is the head of the accounting department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krnojelac, part of the work that you supervised was also seasonal work outside the KP Dom, such as cutting grass or collecting hay, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And even though that wasn't on the premises of the KP Dom or at the farm, that was still within your authority as part of your job, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Novica Mojovic, head of the farm, was in charge of that work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were responsible for Mr. Mojovic, right? You were his -- you were above him in the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he, and therefore you, would be responsible if people, let's say detainees, were taken out to do that kind of work, you would be responsible for making sure that they returned safely, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The safe return was the responsibility of the one who provided the security those -- for those people who had gone out to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if they are doing work for you, aren't you also responsible for their safety, both while they are working and getting there and coming back? That's also your responsibility, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in any event, it is the responsibility of the one who gave them work and the one who takes care of them, and as a man, if you speak about humane relations, then of course, I'm responsible for everyone, but if we talk about this in terms of duty, it is the one who authorised them to do this work and the one who provided security for those men are responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a group of detainees were taken out to gather hay and something bad happened to them there - they were injured or indeed if people failed to return to the KP Dom - that would be your responsibility to find out what happened to them, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't be my responsibility, because it wasn't I who authorised their going there, nor did I assign any job to them. It would be the responsibility of the one who took them out. And heaven forbid a snake bite or perhaps a cut, then regardless of whether it would be my responsibility or not, then of course I would have done my utmost to save his life, and I'd do whatever I could do, but as for all the rest, I do not think I had any responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a group of detainees were taken out to pick plums - that's the kind of seasonal work we are discussing - and failed to return, you would be responsible for finding out what happened to them, right? That fell under your jurisdiction, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, please, I do not really know why we adjourned this session when I put it very precisely whose competence it was. Believe me, I simply do not know who sent them to do what they did, nor do I know what happened to them, and you evidently have some principle to attribute it all to me. It wasn't my responsibility at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, no detainees were actually being used to pick plums at this time, because the orchards were all mined, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that some parts of the orchard were mined in some places because -- in the direction of Scepan Polje, there was a whole orchard which belonged to the cooperative and with apple trees. I don't know how many times I went by, nobody had ever picked those apples, which means it was mined, and other places where were the mines -- where there were no mines, believe me I do not know because I was not a military person nor did I go to those positions so I cannot know whether they were mined or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my brain serves me, I think that a witness too said about that incident, he -- we called it plum picking, so I really know nothing about that. I don't even know when my heart will fail me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, during your interview with the investigators, you said that all the orchards were mined at this time, and that's why it would have been impossible for anybody to be taken to pick plums or any other fruit, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps that is how it was interpreted but I did not say that all the orchards, I said that there were some orchards that had been mined and that could not be entered. If a farmer did not go somewhere to pick fruit, then nobody else should go there because he then knows that it had been mined and won't go in to pick anything, I mean the farmer. And I didn't go there, all over those places, to know that every single orchard had been mined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never -- there was never a part of the Drina Economic Unit work duty that people go pick fruit, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. Never. Nor was there any need for the Drina to go and pick fruit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you knew that detainees were being taken out of the KP Dom either for exchange or -- in any event, never returned, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know why do you claim that I knew about every exchange or about some exchanges? I could hear about them only after the fact, after the exchange, when this exchange has been carried through and then somebody, either from the administration or somebody else, you go out or you sit down or -- and he tells you or she tells you there was an exchange last week. I never knew about this because, you have to understand, I told you whose responsibility it was, and I told you that it was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. transmitted from one person to the other, as for the military command and those other parts, and I had enough work of my own and difficult private life and all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you said somebody from the administration. What do you mean by "the administration"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those clerks who worked in the Drina Economic Unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You learned about -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Kuo, I don't want to suggest that you should hurry, but have you got any idea of how long your cross-examination is going to take? The Trial Chamber is concerned about these other two witnesses that we had hoped to call this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was hoping to finish today, but at this rate, I'm not optimistic about that. But I understand -- we've had discussions with the Defence that we could bring the witnesses in this afternoon at 2.30, in the middle of the testimony of the accused, so that they can be finished today and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's the Defence witness and the Prosecution witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes. And then if we are sitting tomorrow, we can resume and I anticipate finishing the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are only concerned about those two witnesses who I understand, or at least one of them, is not available. She was going to be available on Monday but apparently is no longer available. Mr. Bakrac, have you any views about interrupting your client's evidence for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, insofar as the Defence is concerned, but may I have a minute to check with the accused, who is under oath now, to explain to him what this is about? But the Defence does not object and our expert witness can be here at half past 2.00 and the witness already knows about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We would not do anything without your client's consent and you may certainly speak to him during the adjournment about that. It's only a matter, I think, of trying to dispose of those two witnesses -- I hope that doesn't sound evil -- so that they can get away. Otherwise, apparently we can't hear them until the week of the 16th - I think it's the 16th - of July. But we would not put any pressure on you; it's just a matter that if it can be done, we would like it to be done but we certainly would not override any objection which you or your client would have. So let us know, if you could, at half past 11.00 what your attitude is. We will adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, are you able to given us any indication about this interruption in your client's evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have talked to my client, consulted him, and he doesn't mind, if that will help us move on more efficiently towards the end of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are very grateful to you, Mr. Krnojelac, for so agreeing, and you, Mr. Bakrac, for sorting it out with him. Well, then, we will take your witness, Mr. Bakrac, at 2.30, that's your expert, and the Prosecution's expert should be in court so that she can hear the evidence and give any assistance that's needed for the purposes of cross-examination; and then your expert, Mr. Bakrac, should remain, if she can, to assist you in cross-examination of the Prosecution witness. But you do have the Prosecution witness's statement now so that you should put anything to your witness from that statement that you want her to deal with. We don't want to have to call your witness in reply again, if it can be at all avoided. Right. Yes, Ms. Kuo, you proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you spoke with [redacted] on the day that he was brought back from Cajnice at the end of June 1992, and he told you that they had been brought there and that the exchange had failed, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just don't know whether it was the end of June. I think it was earlier. But at any rate, I did talk to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also learned, after a group of detainees were returned from Niksic, that that exchange had not worked either, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I later on found out that the group got back from Niksic. I found out only a few days afterwards that the group returned from Niksic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew during this time that there were groups being taken out for exchange, right? Or at least, groups of detainees were being taken out; sometimes they were returned and sometimes they weren't?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about these two groups, that they were returned, and, again, I know that this other group was taken to Niksic. I don't know about the others. I heard sometimes that after the exchange would take place, I would find out a couple of days later. Sometimes I would find out and sometimes I wouldn't find out at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was another group taken out for exchange at the end of August, on the 30th of August, that was returned, and that group included your former colleague RJ, who told you what had happened, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He did not tell me about it at all, and I don't know that this group returned. Does that refer to the group that was returned after Niksic? Nobody told me about it because I just heard that Pero Elez returned them from some place before Niksic. My colleague did not tell me that. At that time, I did not see my colleague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know that your colleague was taken out the next day and he was exchanged, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You met several times with your colleague RJ while he was detained at the KP Dom, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you must have also been aware of the circumstances of his release, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have no idea what happened to your friend and colleague, RJ, how it was he was no longer --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know. I did not know. I just knew that Mr. Dakic was asking for him to be released. How he managed to get him released, or rather, how he went for an exchange, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never told RJ when he told you that -- let me rephrase that. You never said, "I thought as much," in response to the description given to you by RJ about how the initial exchange had failed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that these exchanges were done pursuant to lists that were given to the person on duty at the booth, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is learned later. Once I asked on the basis of what were these people taken out, and they told me that a list would arrive, their names would be called out, and they would go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever find out where these lists were compiled or who compiled them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I did not. Nor do I know who compiled them or who gave proposals as to who would go for exchanges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the list would arrive at the KP Dom, the guards at the KP Dom would go get the detainees and assemble them to be taken out, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the procedure involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described how you learned that the lists would arrive. Who told you this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually when somebody would tell me that there was an exchange, I would be interested sometimes as to how this was effected. And then once a man said to me -- if I'm not mistaken, there was a Cancar, Milenko. I asked him about it, and he said to me, "Milorad, a list would arrive, it would be read out, and these people would be taken out for an exchange," and then these people would be taken out for an exchange. I can't remember exactly which period this was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Milenko Cancar who told you this was a policeman at the KP Dom, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked in the Security Service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the same thing as a policeman; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that day he wasn't on duty when I asked him about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nevertheless, his function during the war from April 1992 until the time you left was as a policeman in security of the KP Dom, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked in security, and from when until when, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The Prosecution will draw the Court's attention to Exhibit P3, that Milenko Cancar is listed at 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cancar told you what he did about the list because you were interested, right? You've told us that you were interested.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him whether a few days ago a group was taken for an exchange, and he said yes. And I said, "Well, please tell me how did this take place?" And he said, "As far as I know, there was a list, it was brought in, people were taken out, and they were taken for an exchange."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you ask him further where the list came from and how it was compiled?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask him further. I didn't ask him anything further. This was in passing in front of the KP Dom. I don't know whether he was in more of a hurry or me, but I didn't ask him anything else because, in a way, it occurred to me that this list had to come from the outside, most probably from the military command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did that occur to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I thought at that moment, because that part of the KP Dom had been rented out to the military command and that they were disposing with these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're telling us that your curiosity about this matter stopped at that point, that you never asked anybody further where these lists were coming from?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I said that we just met in passing. One of us was in a hurry. We didn't really stay long, and it's not that we could have talked about it in more detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you never asked anybody else about where these lists came from, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You learned from your colleague RJ that detainees were disappearing overnight, right? He told you that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleague never told me that, or did I ever find out about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never learned that there were people who simply disappeared from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Surely you noticed that the numbers of detainees were going down based on the food supplies that were necessary, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. No one ever told me that, nor could I find out about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never knew that the numbers of Muslim detainees were decreasing during the months of June and July?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true you knew the exact number of detainees who were in the KP Dom in the beginning of June?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not accessible to me at all. It's not that I could have known about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to be clear about this: You're telling us that you had no idea what the number of Muslim detainees was in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 17th of September, you were in the KP Dom when the group of people allegedly being taken for plum picking passed through the yard, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I don't know at all where I was on the 17th of September, but I certainly do not know about this group, that it was taken, or did I see them at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying you also never learned about this group that everybody has been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard about such a group or did I learn about this plum picking until I read about it in the statements that you gave me here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying, sir, that it never happened, or that it could have happened but no one ever told you about it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for anything I did not see with my own eyes or hear with my own ears, I cannot make any assertions in respect of that. The only thing I can assert is that I did not hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you can't say where you were on the 17th of September, 1992, can you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly can't say. I can't even say whether I was at the KP Dom at all on that day because to know such a day very precisely, I mean, it could have been a Saturday or a Sunday, I could have been away over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did not work on Saturdays or Sundays, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one in the economic unit worked on Saturdays and Sundays, the Drina Economic Unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never signed any documents, therefore, on a Saturday or a Sunday?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not have signed anything if I was not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, you never took documents elsewhere or were given documents to sign on a Saturday or a Sunday, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for that, and I do not recall anyone having brought me a document to sign on a Saturday or a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the date on a document that has your signature would be accurate, right, as being the date that you signed it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it should be, but it doesn't have to be that way necessarily. A date could be put that actually pertained to the day after that or the day before that. It depends on when it was written, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, the date that's on a document is the date that it's written, then, not necessarily the day that you signed it. Is that what you're saying? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, yes. There is that possibility, but I'm not asserting that because I don't know which document we are talking about or anything else about that. There is such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Talking about the general procedures, since you mentioned that you weren't present on a Saturday or Sunday. The date on a document is the date the document was written. That would be accurate, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you passed on specific requests from Muslim detainees for release, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were requests that I passed on. I admit that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
