utterances.text: I think that Madam Folnegovic asked the same question, but the way I understood your question is as follows: I described the structure of personality of the tested person, the level of his intellectual functioning, and I understood this model of behaviour to be that it applies to the level of functioning, and I think that what I have mentioned in my opinion, and which relates to the occasional anxiety and panic attacks, is not something that should be qualified as a psychiatric case, nor treated as a psychiatric -- if I fail to understand that, I think we can sit together and try to find an agreement, but perhaps this is a good moment to point out that it is a psychologist that is the right person to measure the level of functioning, that is, how a person defends himself, how it solves uncomfortable, difficult situations. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I did the best I could in the environment that I could, but I don't think that it ever rises to the level of being a mental disease, and I think this is how I understood my colleague's position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that it is -- you're not comfortable with trying to second-guess Madam Folnegovic's own analysis. I think it is better that -- if she is asked herself. However, I just wanted to expedite matters and jump a little bit ahead. So I only have one more question of you. On page 12 of Madam Folnegovic's opinion, in paragraph 2, it states that Mr. Krnojelac was likely -- that he uses the mechanisms of denial and suppression after having first complied with the orders of his superiors. Does that strike you as something that is a rational type of behaviour? Am I right in reading it that way?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Again, I believe that Dr. Folnegovic is a better person to ask -- answer that, but as I'm the first person who is giving evidence here, and I can only give you my perception and my view of it. Conditionally, this is perhaps just an awkward way of putting it, and this is not an objection really. And I think that Dr. Folnegovic will also agree with a commonly-known fact in psychology that defence mechanisms develop as the person develops. It is not something that is found in the, in the person beforehand. It is not something that is part of a rational mechanism, so it may have just been that this sentence was structured in such a way that it left you with this impression. But I believe that the denial and repression is something that is happened -- has happened with our patient. And also, the isolation of affects in situations when he cannot control the situation, this is what is triggered off in order to restore the balance in his personality and his previous functioning. This is, at least, how I understand it. However, I do allow that Madam Folnegovic may add something else to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Najman.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has no more questions in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Najman.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Najman, you mentioned that you testified -- you mentioned that you testified in the case against Mladjo Radic. You actually testified in March of this year, right?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic is a Serb indicted for having participated as shift commander in the mistreatment of Muslim detainees in the Omarska camp, right?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not want to dispute or challenge any of your findings in relation to Mr. Radic; it's not, it's not our case here. However, I want to discuss a few similarities between your findings there and in this case here. If you need the findings of Mr. Radic, we have it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not want to enter them into evidence; therefore, I did not provide a submission like this. I just want to discuss a few sentences of this expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I don't want to stop you, but I'm curious to know just how this gets us anywhere. Let's assume that she says exactly the same as to Mr. Radic. What does that have to do with us here?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I want to stress a few points in relation to increased anxiety and this increased receptiveness to orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do we need to know very much about what Mr. Radic did or is alleged to have done?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We're not going into any of these difficult -- in any of these details. I just want to read two, three sentences from this expertise to show that it's actually the same findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of that rather alluring promise to be brief, you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I have here for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies. The Defence is a bit concerned because we don't know where this is going. The expert chosen by the Prosecutor found -- came to the same findings, so I don't know what this finding is to show. It is from another case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But Mr. Vasic, that is one of the great mysteries and sometimes the enjoyment of a cross-examination. Neither you nor the witness know where it's headed. I think the Trial Chamber has to accept from counsel with the experience of Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff that she can't take it too far.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I, myself, have queried it, but I think let's see where she goes. If we see that she's going right off the rails, which would be unexpected, then you may renew your objection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Najman, I have here your expertise in the B/C/S language, and I just want to cite a very few sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you said you have her expertise. You mean her expert report or the statement of her qualifications?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. The written expertise dated the 7th of May, 2000, in the case for Mladjo Radic. That is her findings on -- her written findings on Mr. Mladjo Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, please, here is the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your finding, you also have the chapter "Description of Personality." Can you please look at --

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the English version, it's page 5, and in the B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it's page 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, in the third paragraph, the last sentence, you mention, "There is increased insecurity, anxiety, and distrust towards new situations and persons." Do you see that, the third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. After your definitions of symbols, there is the next paragraph, and the last sentence is what I just read out to you, right?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I see the increased insecurity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the next paragraph, actually, you write, "This personality is characterised by the following traits: loyalty, modesty, passivity, servility, sensitivity, and a high degree of conformism." In paragraph 6 of this same chapter, you write, "The dimensions of obedience, gullibility, dependence, and suggestibility are pronounced." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And actually, as the last, as the last paragraph of your findings, you highlight, "The conformity and acceptance as his social conduct, behavioural motive which emerges from the need to behave like others and as they expect one to behave." Do you see that? It's shortly after this two separate little dashes with sentences after, then there comes it.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these are --

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: It sounds very different in English than in Serbo-Croatian, so have had some difficulty finding it, but I did find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So these were, what I just read to you, these were your findings in your relation to Mr. Radic, right? Now we come to your evaluation of Mr. Krnojelac. In chapter 3, from recollection, it's on page 3, you mentioned the wounding of the son, the sons of Mr. Krnojelac - it's actually paragraph 3 of this - and you say, "Their wounding was emotionally difficult and hard for him to accept."

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, emotionally, yes. It was difficult for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he not sad about it, and at the same time, accepted it as consequence of the war? Do you recall what he actually said?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I think if we have the same thing in mind, I think he said, "Well, that's the war." That is the sentence that he repeated often, if that is what you mean. But I don't know, perhaps I can have a look, because here I have the originals from Mr. Krnojelac's case history and perhaps I can find his exact words if I misquoted him, if that was what you had in mind. Or could you perhaps help me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think you do not need to search that in your notes because, actually, in the expertise of Mrs. Folnegovic, you find that she actually cites him saying, "That is the war." The wounding of the son, "That's the war," which is what you yourself remembered now. And Mrs. Folnegovic, in her expertise, also mentioned that he said, "I would give everything for the war not to have happened but when it did, there is no other way than to accept it." Do you recall him saying that or kind of something like this?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Of course, yes, because we were together throughout the examination, so of course I heard that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also Mrs. Folnegovic gave in her expertise the -- in her written expertise, the sentence in relation how he thinks about the war, "May it be in the home of the one who wants it but when it comes -- when it does come, it should be accepted. War has its own, and that's how it is." Do you also recall this?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I do, yes, I remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A man who says something like this would join the war effort when he is asked to do so, right? He would accept it because it's how it is, right?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps. Perhaps he would come to the terms with the fact and say, "Well, the war has happened and we all have to suffer it." There is also that kind of reaction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not only suffer it but participate if you are asked to do that. Isn't that his position?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Well, I do not mean -- I mean to tolerate it. When I say "to suffer it," I mean to tolerate it. "We are in that situation, there is this war, you cannot change anything, and you have to put up with it." That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Krnojelac actually, when you look at what he told you about himself during the war, he actually did participate. When he was called up, he went immediately to the high school and, yeah, took his duty, right?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, he assumed that duty requested of him, in view of the duties that he -- obligations that he had, not as an active-duty military, as far as I can understand from what he told me, but it was an obligation which he understood as a labour duty. That is, I think, how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A person with Mr. Krnojelac's personality would actually feel the duty to help his people and to do what he is tasked with, right? He has such a personality?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Well, I did mention it today, I believe, and I think you will find it in the finding, he has those characteristics of a passive personality and characteristics of a person who obeys, who will bend to authority, up to a certain level. When he cannot cope with it any longer - and I believe I explained it today - when he cannot cope with it, then he starts to procrastinate, to hesitate, he is increasingly passive and often simply withdraws from such situations. It seems to me -- it's just occurred to me as we are talking about this, I think he even said that at some point he also asked to be relieved of this obligation, of this labour duty, and that is how I understand it, psychologically, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Folnegovic also mentioned in her written expertise that the accused, in relation to the military part of the KP Dom, said, and here I quote from page 9 of the English version, "He did not care about what was happening in the other part of the KP Dom, that nobody informed him about" -- there is some problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We have a picture but no transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [English] We have no picture again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We seem to have both. You proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. But I think I'll read this part again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the military part of the KP Dom, Mrs. Folnegovic wrote, "He did not care about what was happening in the other part of the KP Dom, that nobody informed him about any beatings or torture, and that he did not ask anybody," and she further cited him as, "I was" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: One moment. There are a lot of problems. I can see the interpreters are having troubles too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was I too fast?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, just no sound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [English] And no translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And no translation for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can I start?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "He did not care about what was happening" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [English] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This may succeed in allowing us to get out of this shoebox into another courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think our microphones were turned on.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, now I do hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, all three booths can hear you. Let's go.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Now I read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "He did not care about what was happening in the other part of the KP Dom, that nobody informed him about any beatings or torture, and that he did not ask anybody." And he is further cited as follows: "I was uninformed about everything and it was not up to me to get involved in it and worry about it. I did my job, they did theirs, that is what war is like." Do you recall him saying that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I do, yes, yes, absolutely. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would you say that this attitude is rather the attitude of a narrow-minded person?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I followed it well, because of the technical problems, what my learned friend has read out to Mrs. Najman and the quotation and the question, I think that there are several sentences missing here as this quotation -- as this text was read out. I stand to be corrected but I don't think I'm wrong. I think that the quotation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: She may not have read every word but every word she read out is in the report and that's the -- the cross-examiner is entitled to say, "These particular statements, do they indicate something?" If you want to, in re-examination, and you think there is something else in the report which would be relevant, you can ask the witness whether the other material would change her mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour, thank you. But I -- it seems to me that the meaning is thereby slightly altered. That is why I objected, because if the accused -- the words of the accused are quoted, then I think it would be fair to quote all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Only if it alters the context. I haven't checked it word for word. But Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, rather than leaving it open to get a different answer in re-examination, read -- there is only one paragraph there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, it's a longer one. And I just picked out a few sentences from this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The trouble is, when you read, everything goes wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Today, at least today. So I read the entire paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "He says that he had nothing to do with the military part. 'I did not have the time nor the possibility to find out about certain things. I worked between seven and 15 hours a day, practically without a break.' He says that he did not care about what was happening in the other part of the Dom, that nobody informed him --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel read a little bit slower so the interpreters can catch up?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "... that nobody informed him about any beatings or torture and that he did not ask anybody. Only later did he hear some things, but while he worked there he knew nothing about any of this. 'I was uninformed about everything and I was not up -- it was not up to me to get involved in it and worry about it. I did my job, they did theirs. What is -- that is what war is like. The army and the military command took care of those who were detained, not I.'" It continues but is that enough? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. I've found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my additional question was: This attitude expressed by the accused speaks for a rather narrow-minded personality, right? Wouldn't you say, though, the person says that, "it's not my thing to worry about it"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, the problem is your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. expression "narrow-minded personality." That bears one meaning. Do you mean narrowly-focused personality?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, completely focused on his -- what he is doing and not caring about anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, from a purely English point of view, that makes better sense to me, but it may be different for the psychiatrists and the psychologists, and it may even be different between the two of them, but try that one and see how you go.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree to this? That he is completely focused on himself and what he is doing and ignores ...

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Well, you see, now that you read this passage, it sounds slightly differently now that you read it out and I listen to it than when I wrote it down. I cannot escape from the fact that I'm a psychologist, as Your Honours have said, and I look at him and a personality in toto. So I wouldn't say that he is a narrow-minded man or a man who is focused on himself. I think it has to do with his intellectual abilities, and I spoke about it. I mentioned it. Perhaps I didn't emphasise it enough, but he lacks curiosity, he lacks exploring spirit. He does not wish to know new things, and that derives from his primary, general, intellectual potential. And at least I as a psychologist would attribute it rather to that than an attitude. An attitude is something else. At this point in time, that is what it looks like to me, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 of your expertise in relation to -- from recollection, chapter from recollection, you mentioned that the accused continued his professional education to become a subject teacher, although it was not his wish -- did you find it? Do you remember? It's on page 3 on the bottom. Yes? Do you remember that he said that it was not his wish actually to do that, but he accepted it and fulfilled it then, right? Also, it was not his wish. He accepted it and fulfilled his education as suggested, right?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: You see, now perhaps I could interpret what Mr. Krnojelac told us and what it sounded like to me as a psychologist. He came out of the teachers academy, and he taught children. He liked mathematics or, rather, calculus, as he liked to say, and the opportunity arose to receive further education and thus acquired the formal education in mathematics, and so he seized that opportunity. So he did not choose, did not go to attend a higher school by taking a decision because the -- his family lived in very poor material conditions, in very dire straits. He was already married, if I'm right, had one or two children, and he simply could not afford to enjoy university and stop working. That is how I interpreted it. And I do not think it is the result of the absence of a wish or will to do it but just due to these circumstances which were such as they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in paragraph 5 of your chapter of recollection, you mentioned, actually, although it was not his wish, he did that. So it has something to do with his wishes. He didn't have the wish; that's what you gave here.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes. But you know, I thought I had explained it. It's not that he had no wish, it was simply very difficult circumstances of his life. He had to take care of his family, of providing for them rather than about what he wanted to do or didn't want to do. It's not that there was no wish. Perhaps I'm not being clear enough, but at least that is how I understood it, and I think that if Mrs. Folnegovic was present there, she can tell us also how she understood that. That is how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Folnegovic actually gave in her report to other similar situations, and I want to put them to you. Mrs. Folnegovic wrote that in 1973, he became a member of the communist party by decree. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also she wrote that, again by decree, he was transferred to the Veselin Maslesa school. So again, that it is not his decision. Someone else makes the decision, and he does it. Accepts it and does it. Is that, is that not the typical conformist behaviour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Both reports described it as being conformist. I don't know what this is leading to. There's no dispute between them at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I want to come to the point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, let's get to the point, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in your -- today, you mentioned -- today you mentioned that he did not have the typical advancement and educational and professional development. It was kind of extraordinary. Was it faster than usual?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: No, no, no. I do not think that it was faster. He completed his schooling in 1973 when he was about 30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it was not the usual way to do it. He at the same time had his job, education, but already worked in the job. How is that to explain?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps the term "unusual" may not be the best expression, but I can explain what I meant. Somebody goes to the school, finishes school, finds a job and starts working. In Mr. Krnojelac's case, it was -- there were both things, but the sequence was not followed. That's what I meant. Common or not common, that is simply my impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You noticed that he had this increased anxiety and fear, and you also described why he had this in the test situation. A lot of persons would react in such situations in a similar way, right? It's not unusual what he experienced and what you saw on him.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said. I think I said it today, that testing one's intelligence or testing the intellectual abilities of somebody is always frustrating, more or less, and I think that Mr. Krnojelac was slightly more frustrated, that is that anxiety was higher, and I confirm it by the fact that the test -- that I interrupted this testing and we came back to it the next day and we gave him some water and sugar and that, but now that we are drawing comparisons with Mr. Radic, for instance, that never happened there. The testing went all right from beginning to end. That is, there were no interruptions due to some such things as we are talking about now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I hope it's not a sign of either anxiety or frustration, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, but how much longer is this cross-examination going to go on, bearing in mind that the findings of both of the experts are almost identical?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: They differ in one rather particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When are we going to get to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have to build, I have to come to this, but it will be 20 more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, dear. Well, we can't resume until 11.30 tomorrow because we have a number of other matters listed already which we could not defer so we will resume again tomorrow morning at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
